documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                          )
Interconnection of Large Loads                            )                Docket No. RM26-4-000
to the Interstate Transmission System                     )

       REPLY COMMENTS OF THE PEW CHARITABLE TRUSTS, ENERGY
      MODERNIZATION PROJECT ON THE ADVANCE NOTICE OF PROPOSED
                           RULEMAKING

        The Pew Charitable Trusts (Pew) submits these reply comments in response to the

Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANOPR) on Ensuring the Timely and Orderly

Interconnection of Large Loads.1 Pew’s Energy Modernization Project works with state and

federal policymakers to build a modern, reliable, and affordable electric grid, including the

adoption of local, distributed energy, such as home solar and batteries.

        While commenters disagree on the question whether the Commission should take

jurisdiction over the interconnection of large load customers to the transmission system (a

question which Pew takes no position on), they are united on the imperative to speed up

interconnection processes while preserving affordability for existing customers.2 Many

commenters endorse the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) proposed principles designed to

achieve these goals: coordinated study of load and generation, as well as expedited

interconnection for large load customers and hybrid facilities.3

        In addition, the evidence in the record demonstrates that Virtual Power Plants

(VPPs) can be integrated into implementation of these principles, and that providing for

 large load customers and hybrid facilities to be able to contract with VPPs and to have

those contracts accounted for within the scope of interconnection procedures would greatly

further DOE’s goals, while advancing the Commission’s statutory mandate and principles

of facilitating resource-neutral competition in wholesale markets. Including VPPs within the

scope of the rule is consistent with Commission precedent dictating that aggregations of

Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) should be permitted to offer services that they are

technically capable of providing, and could be done without expanding on the scope of the

Commission’s jurisdictional claim or intruding upon state-jurisdictional VPP programs.4 Given

the scale of the challenge that DOE and the Commission face in facilitating speed-to-power for

large load customers while keeping the system affordable for existing customers, the

Commission cannot afford not to deploy this important tool. Rather, it should insist that

transmission providers include it within the toolbox and use it for the job at hand.

    I.       TO THE EXTENT THE COMMISSION ASSERTS JURISDICTION IN THIS
             PROCEEDING, IT SHOULD ADOPT RULES TO ENABLE INTEGRATED,
             EXPEDITED INTERCONNECTION STUDY OF LARGE LOADS
             CONTRACTING WITH VIRTUAL POWER PLANT OPERATORS TO
             CURTAIL OR DISPATCH.


             A. Accounting for contracts between large load customers and VPPs in the
                interconnection process could help to expedite interconnection for large load
                customers while reducing system costs for all customers, goals that are widely
                supported by commenters.

         The ANOPR proposes that “[l]oad and hybrid facilities should be studied together with

generation facilities,”5 and states that “FERC should expedite interconnection study of large

loads that agree to be curtailable and hybrid facilities that agree to be curtailable and

Sys. Operators, Order No. 2222, 172 FERC ¶ 61,247, at P 26 (2020), order on reh'g, Order No. 2222-A,
174 FERC ¶ 61,197, order on reh’g, Order No. 2222-B, 175 FERC ¶ 61,227 (2021).
5
  ANOPR at P 20.


                                                        2
 dispatchable.”6 To the extent that it asserts jurisdiction over large load and hybrid facility

interconnection through this proceeding, the Commission should adopt and clarify these

proposals. In doing so, the Commission should ensure that large load customers are able to

contract with VPPs that curtail or dispatch. A broad range of commenters support including VPPs

within the scope of the Commission’s rules,7 emphasizing how VPP’s can be a critical tool in

achieving DOE’s objectives and supporting the Commission’s statutory mission of ensuring just

and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory rates. Adopting rules that allow integrated,

expedited study of large loads that contract with VPPs will facilitate speed-to-power for large

load customers while keeping transmission and energy affordable for existing customers.

         Secretary of Energy Wright’s letter directing the Commission to consider the ANOPR

emphasizes the need to “ensure efficient, timely and non-discriminatory load interconnections,”

while guaranteeing that “all Americans and domestic industries have access to affordable,

reliable, and secure electricity.”8 Achieving these twin goals simultaneously is challenging

because serving large loads requires the rapid addition of new capacity resources and

transmission system upgrades, which are costly and time consuming to build. Under the status

quo, none of the Secretary’s objectives will be realized: large loads will face continuing delays

connecting to the grid while electricity becomes more expensive and less reliable for existing

 customers. For example, comments filed from Distributed Capacity Parties emphasize that

“[l]arge loads face interconnection delays for several reasons, including insufficient capacity to

supply new load reliably,” and “the need for costly network upgrades to bring incremental peak

power to the location of new load.”9

        A large majority of commenters who address large load flexibility support the concept of

expedited interconnection for curtailable large load customers and curtailable and dispatchable

hybrid facilities. AEMA tallies more than a hundred comments in support as compared to just

over a dozen “cautionary voices.”10 Enabling flexibility, in practice, however, will require an all-

hands-on-deck approach.11 This includes utility-scale hybrid generation facilities and energy

storage,12 demand response,13 VPPs and DERs,14 and data center flexibility management

software solutions.15 The exact mix depends on the type of large load facility and its unique

circumstances.

        Given the scale of large load growth, and the variety of contexts in which large loads may

seek interconnection service, it is important to provide as many tools as possible to enable

flexibility—thereby unlocking more megawatts (MWs) of flexibility and making flexibility

available to a broader set of commercial entities. The scale of the opportunity that VPPs could

provide to support large load flexibility is significant: “In 2023 alone,” for example, Distributed

Capacity Parties note that “Southwest Power Pool (‘SPP’) added approximately 431 MW new

America emphasizes that “[h]yperscalers could meet one third of their projected additional

capacity needs by paying for heat pumps in select households that currently use inefficient

electric heating, cooling, and water heating,” and “could more than meet their total planned

capacity needs by paying for battery storage as well as rooftop solar for homes well suited for

it.”17 In addition, VPPs can be integrated with other solutions. As Emerald AI explains in their

comments, VPPs “complement . . . -[other] types of data center flexibility to . . . augment the

total flexibility a facility can offer.”18 This is especially true for data centers “located in very

close proximity to financial sector, national security, or other critical uses that demand the

absolute minimum security risk and data latency.”19 By allowing “[t]hose data centers located in

dense metropolitan areas . . . to tap into the wealth of flexibility opportunities that surround

them,”20 the Commission can facilitate speed-to-power and consumer protections that might not

be available if the Commission limited hybrid facility fast tracks only to large loads contracting

with utility-scale resources.

        In addition to enabling simpler and faster interconnection study, VPPs can facilitate

speed-to-power because they are much faster to deploy than utility-scale infrastructure,

minimizing potential construction and supply chain delays that have exacerbated resource

adequacy challenges and transmission system headroom scarcity. As commenters explain, the

core challenge facing transmission providers across the country is that new load is being added

to the system faster than new supply can interconnect. While grid operators across the country

and appear likely to continue to remain clogged at least in the near term. VPPs, by contrast, do

not depend on proceeding through the large generator interconnection queue. As Distributed

Capacity Parties explain, “[d]istributed capacity assets are installed today across critical

footprints, are readily installable en masse, and may be aggregated into utility-scale assets on a

timeline of months rather than years” (emphasis added).21

             B. Commission precedent supports including VPPs within the scope of any
                interconnection rule, because they are technically capable of providing the
                same system value as direct curtailment or dispatch of the large load or
                hybrid facility.

        VPPs are technically capable of providing the same interconnection service benefits as

direct facility curtailment and dispatch. As such, Commission precedent supports including them

within the scope of any rule providing for joint or coordinated study of load and generation,

and/or expedited interconnection for curtailable and dispatchable facilities.

        As Rewiring America emphasizes, “[o]ff-site distributed energy resources (‘DERs’) can

deliver the same types of energy services—generation, load reduction, or transmission relief—

that on-site assets provide.”22 From the resource adequacy perspective, Rewiring America notes

that “demand-side measures that permanently lower peak load[,]” which can include both

reliance on DERs to enable curtailed consumption from network resources and coordinated

distributed demand reduction to offset large load needs, “can meaningfully reduce the system

impacts of new large loads.”23 Distributed Capacity Parties also note the ability of virtual power

plants to increase transmission system utilization and save on network upgrades, including

through the use of “‘latent’ demand flexibility [to] meet incremental capacity needs by reducing


21
   Distributed Capacity Parties Joint Comments at 3 (emphasis added).
22
   Rewiring America Comments at 2.
23
   Id. at 3.

 power draw from the grid, thereby freeing up network capacity.”24 In order to provide these

transmission system benefits, Rewiring America highlights that “[l]ocational requirements can

ensure these resources provide benefits on the same part of the grid affected by the

interconnection.”25 The key point is that when VPPs curtail and dispatch, this can provide the

same system benefits as when a large load does so directly. As Rewiring America points out,

“[W]hat matters is equivalent, verifiable performance in mitigating constraints within the same

constrained transmission pocket or local grid area, not whether the asset is physically inside or

outside the facility fence line.”26 In a similar vein, Equinix explains, “[s]o long as a large load is

contracted with and can deliver a solution that resolves or mitigates the constraints and violations

that would otherwise trigger incremental energy system costs, that aggregated proposal should be

studied as part of the large load interconnection request.”27

        The same principles underlying Order No. 2222 require the Commission to provide the

opportunity for VPPs to participate in hybrid and flexible arrangements where technically

capable of doing so. Specifically, to the extent that the Commission adopts rules for the

combined or coordinated study of generation and loads, it should require transmission providers

to facilitate a pathway through which VPPs can be accounted for in load interconnection studies

on a comparable basis to utility-scale generation.

        In Order No. 2222, the Commission found that existing regional transmission

organization (RTO)/independent system operator (ISO) market rules were unjust and

unreasonable because they “present[ed] barriers that prevent[ed] certain distributed energy

resources that are technically capable of participating in the RTO/ISO markets on their own or

   Distributed Capacity Parties Joint Comments at 6.

 through aggregation from doing so[,]” which “reduce[d] competition and fail[ed] to ensure just

and reasonable rates.”28 The same non-discrimination principle requires the Commission to allow

aggregated DERs that are technically capable of providing hybrid service to avail themselves of

the opportunities available to utility-scale hybrid facilities. As Equinix explains, “[f]rom a grid

operations, transmission upgrade, or incremental energy need perspective, it is irrelevant whether

a large load is curtailed, backup or other co-located generation reduces the customer’s draw from

the grid, or other load, generation or storage in sufficient proximity reduces draws from the

grid.”29 Just as opening wholesale markets to DER aggregations “enhance[s] the

competitiveness, and in turn the efficiency, of RTO/ISO markets and thereby help[s] to ensure

just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential rates for wholesale electric

services[,]”30 “[e]nabling a wide range of flexible resources” including VPPs “to be paired with

large load interconnection requests would . . . spark competition and innovation” and “enable

lower overall costs and potentially broader benefits.”31 Accordingly, the Commission should

extend the logic of Order No. 2222 to any hybrid-specific large load interconnection rules that it

adopts and allow all resources technically capable of providing the relevant service to participate.

        Neglecting to do so and thereby excluding resources that are similarly situated in their

technical ability to provide the relevant service and benefits from participating in the hybrid-

specific procedures would clearly raise questions of undue discrimination.


            C. Rules leveraging the value of technically-capable VPPs to facilitate
               interconnection are compatible with a broad range of implementation
               frameworks set forth by commenters.

29

         Accordingly, if the Commission adopts rules providing for joint or coordinated study of

large loads with generation supply and expediting integrated interconnection study for large load

and hybrid resources it should require transmission providers to enable VPPs to contribute and

be accounted for in these rules. Specifically, the Commission should define hybrid facility in a

manner that includes large loads paired with VPPs and/or allow for large load customers and

hybrid facilities to contract with VPPs or coordinate operations with jointly-owned VPPs in

order to provide curtailment and/or dispatch capability. This point stands regardless of how the

Commission proceeds from the ANOPR, whether fully standardizing large load interconnection

procedures, adopting a more limited set of requirements specific to flexible loads, or adopting

even more limited requirements applicable only to hybrids.

        Commenters have pointed out that two types of impacts of large load and hybrid facility

additions may be accounted for through this rule: (1) the impact of these facilities on supply

resource needs; and (2) the impact of these facilities on the transmission system. To the extent

that the Commission addresses either type of impact, VPPs can and should be leveraged to offset

both of these types of impacts in a large load interconnection rule.

        VPPs’ greatest value in this context may be their ability to offset the supply resource

needs created by large load customers (e.g. Network Resource requirements in order to

interconnect and obtain transmission service, as well as resource adequacy requirements).

Various proposals recommend jointly studying or providing for coordinated study of large load

customers with associated capacity supply, expediting interconnection of resources that bring

their own capacity, or conditioning interconnection of large loads on bringing their own

capacity.32 Should the Commission adopt such a proposal or develop a similar framework, it


32

or addition of new generation by load to meet their energy needs); Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate and

 should ensure that VPPs are eligible to provide capacity for these interconnection study

purposes.

         For example, Industrial Customer Organizations advocate for the implementation of an

elective “Fast Lane Interconnection” for customers who, among other criteria, “can add new

generation to the system . . . .”33 Similarly, Critical Loop recommends that the Commission

“[r]ecognize [Large Load Flexibility Commitments (LLFCs)] for capacity/resource adequacy

(capacity accreditation or reduced procurement obligations), enabling faster energization when

capacity constraints would otherwise delay interconnection.”34 Distributed Capacity Parties

suggest that “[n]ew large loads that bring their own capacity—in whatever form—should be

studied together with that capacity.”35 As Critical Loop and Distributed Capacity Parties

emphasize, these proposals could be implemented to “explicitly include study of incremental

resources in the relevant grid area, whether or not those resources look like traditional utility-

scale power plants.”36 Aggregated DERs across the relevant balancing authority are capable of

reducing a large load customer’s capacity impacts in any such cases and should be provided for

in any resulting rule.

         To the extent that the Commission takes action in this proceeding, its approach should

recognize that capacity supply constraints prompted by large load additions to the system are a

key part of the need for reform.37 Likewise, the Commission should recognize the multiple

that are willing to bring their own generation”).

interconnection processes for flexible loads contracting with new supply resources should be

divorced from consideration of those large load and hybrid resources’ resource adequacy

impacts,38 these perspectives overlook the unique system challenges that the Commission now

faces. In today’s market conditions, there is a critical link between generator interconnection

study speed and resource adequacy challenges.

         Interconnection rules related to resource adequacy impacts and ensuring that balancing

authorities have adopted operations protocols to enable these interconnection frameworks are

distinct from adopting any nationally-applicable rules for the resource adequacy frameworks

themselves. And while it may be challenging for the Commission to include express

requirements for any modifications to resource adequacy frameworks as part of this ANOPR

given the widely varying nature of resource adequacy requirements and the state-jurisdictional

nature of these requirements in some regions, the Commission could nevertheless encourage

including generation and storage.”).

         Existing resource adequacy constructs may no longer be producing just and reasonable

rates because generator interconnection queue delays prevent new supply from responding to

high prices,39 and integrated reform of both sets of rules may be appropriate. To facilitate this,

the Commission could clarify that such integrated reforms may fall with the scope of a final rule

as “consistent with or superior to” the requirements set forth by the Commission. Recognizing

the ability of flexibility commitments to streamline interconnection study requirements and then

accounting for those (or related) flexibility commitments in resource adequacy planning

appropriately provides speed-to-market for both associated load and supply while keeping rates

just and reasonable for existing customers.

        Second, the Commission should allow VPPs that meet applicable technical requirements

to qualify an associated large load for expedited interconnection service pathways that depend on

transmission system impacts. Various parties have proposed different mechanisms to implement

the ANOPR’s expedited interconnection and integrated load and generation facility study

principles based on the potential for curtailment and dispatch to lead to reduced transmission

system impacts. These include technical eligibility requirements that large load customers or

hybrid facilities would need to meet in order to be eligible for expedited and integrated

interconnection processes. Pew does not take a position on the relative merits of these specific

technical proposals. Regardless of which particular suggestion or combination of suggestions the

Commission ultimately pursues to enable flexibility, or whether it develops its own approach

based on the record, the Commission should adopt resource-neutral definitions that allow VPPs

to satisfy technical requirements where they are able to provide the services that the technical

requirements are designed to ensure.

            For example, Eolian proposes adoption of serial streamlined study of load- and

electrically-close hybrid facilities without carrying out generation and load deliverability analysis

where the facility (1) nominates operating limits for aggregate net injections and withdrawals of

power, (2) installs necessary control equipment to ensure that the facility is capable of following

the dispatch controls of the transmission system operator and balancing authority and respecting

operating limits at all times, and (3) is capable at any time of complete self-supply or otherwise

curtailing the load such that the facility can take transmission service on a non-firm basis.40 VPPs

could be compatible with this type of proposal to the extent that contracts or coordinated

operation with a jointly-owned portfolio of electrically-close DERs enable the facility to meet

the specified operating limits. Where a large load customer’s VPP portfolio allows the combined

resources to meet those technical requirements, that configuration should enable the same

streamlined study. Similarly, Critical Loop urges the Commission to establish a “Large-Load

Flexibility Commitment” (LLFC) construct under which transmission providers would be

required “to model LLFC parameters explicitly in interconnection studies” for a load that

“accepts specified curtailment and/or relies on on-site or adjacent supply under defined

conditions . . . .”41 Aggregated DERs, again, should be eligible as “adjacent supply” in this

example, because they are as able to reduce the new large load’s transmission system impacts as

utility-scale resources.

           Like utility-scale resources paired with large loads, VPPs could receive credit based on

the degree of flexibility they enable. For example, “CAISO recommends that any final rule

should establish distinct ‘lanes’ based on the level of dispatch tools the transmission provider




40
     Eolian, L.P. Comments at 37, 39.
41
     Critical Loop Comments at 2.


                                                   13
 will have—all, some, or none.”42 Because “the specific grid topology will . . . be a key factor,”43

eligibility can flow from the particular system location of DERs that form a VPP and from their

dispatch capabilities. Importantly, studying VPPs together with large loads through a single

integrated process would not mean combining the VPP with the large load and only studying the

net service requirements (a simplification that could inappropriately mask reliability risks).

Rather, as with generation components of a hybrid facility, the streamlined study process could

simply study the VPP and load components together, so that the combined effect of the

components on the system become evident while recognizing that they are separate components

of a broader configuration.44

        A key component of enabling these frameworks is to allow large load customers to

contract with third parties in order to achieve curtailability or dispatchability. As Base Power

recommends, curtailability and dispatchability could “be implemented as defined, contractible

commodities in order to be sufficiently integrated into both operations and system planning.”45

Base Power proposes that “[t]o be contractible, particularly for dispatchable load, the conditions

for operation must be clearly delimited and well-defined, with established parameters for

availability and performance requirements (e.g., ramp rate and target power error tolerances).”46

Clear definition should include specifying when and how VPPs can meet these requirements.

Base Power points to ERCOT’s definition of Controllable Load Resources, which provides one

example of a set of resource-neutral performance metrics that could be adopted.47

             D. Allowing VPPs to be eligible for hybrid programs would not and should not
               intrude on states’ abilities to incentivize VPPs, including those that
               simultaneously benefit a FERC-jurisdictional large load.

        States have justifiably expressed support for VPPs and wish to retain “the ability to

incentivize large loads to invest in local communities, including through programs such as . . .

funding virtual power plants, non-transmission alternatives, or demand-side management

programs.”48 While Pew does not take a position on the question of whether the Commission

should exert jurisdiction over large load interconnection, we emphasize that to the extent the

Commission does so, including VPPs as eligible to contribute to expedited interconnection

through Commission-jurisdictional tariffs would not infringe on the ability of states to require or

encourage investment in VPPs as part of any processes or services that remain state

jurisdictional, including, for example, large load retail service tariffs. Similarly, rendering VPPs

eligible to contribute to large load and hybrid facility interconnection processes would not

override the terms of retail VPP programs. Rather, such programs would remain valid as adopted,

and VPPs would be eligible to support FERC-jurisdictional interconnection service while

simultaneously participating in such a program only to the extent the commitments provided

pursuant to the relevant state program were consistent with the obligations of the VPP pursuant

to the FERC-jurisdictional interconnection agreement of the applicable large load customer or

hybrid facility. Importantly, because FERC’s rule in this context would be to establish an

interconnection process yielding an interconnection agreement and not to compensate resources,

the risk of double counting addressed in FERC Order No. 2222 is not presented in the same

manner in this context. However, to the extent that any FERC regime involves assessing the net



48
  National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners Comments, “Resolution Urging the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission to Preserve and Affirm State Retail Regulatory Jurisdiction in its Large Load
Interconnection Proceeding.”


                                                     15
 impacts of the load plus the VPP, FERC should require transmission providers to ensure that the

VPP’s load reduction potential has not already been factored into the load forecast through a

separate process. In other words, the Commission should ensure that modeling and other aspects

of the interconnection process do not inappropriately double count the impact of the VPP.

   II.      CONCLUSION

         VPPs are critically positioned to allow the timely interconnection of large loads while

protecting existing customers from adverse impacts and allowing for additional benefits. They

are especially well positioned to bring capacity online quickly given their rapid deployment
